body:
Why local observations are needed

Satellites can observe large regions, but district authorities also need recent information about particular roads, buildings and communities. Drones and crowdsourced reports can provide this local detail. They complement satellite observations rather than replacing them.

Drones in disaster management

A drone, or unmanned aircraft, is an aircraft operated without a pilot on board. It may carry cameras or other sensors to collect information from the air.

When fitted with suitable sensors, drones perform a form of airborne remote sensing. Their usefulness comes from obtaining relatively detailed observations of selected places without requiring a surveyor to stand at every observation point.

Common applications

  • Damage assessment: Photographing visibly damaged roads, bridges, roofs and other infrastructure for further examination.
  • Flood observation: Recording the extent of water around selected settlements or transport links.
  • Situational awareness: Providing recent aerial views of places that may be difficult to observe from the ground.
  • Planning and recovery: Comparing local conditions before and after repairs or other recovery activities.

A drone image may reveal a blocked road, but an image by itself cannot certify the strength or safety of a structure. Such conclusions require appropriate inspection and professional judgement.

Limitations and responsible use

Drone operations depend on weather, battery capacity, visibility, communication links, safe operating conditions and applicable airspace requirements. Unauthorised flying can interfere with emergency operations or endanger people. Drone imagery can also reveal private homes and identifiable individuals; collection and sharing must therefore be proportionate and appropriately controlled.

Meaning of crowdsourcing

Crowdsourcing means collecting information or contributions from many people, often through digital or communication platforms.

In disaster management, residents, volunteers or field workers may report flooded streets, damaged assets, blocked routes or urgent local needs. Reports may arrive through mobile applications, telephone calls, messages or organised community networks.

Geotagging attaches location information to an observation. A geotagged photograph can help a district team identify where an incident was reported and compare the report with existing maps.

Why crowdsourced reports must be verified

Reports from affected communities can be timely and valuable, but several problems are possible:

  • Multiple people may report the same incident, leading to duplication.
  • A photograph may have been taken on an earlier date or at another location.
  • The reported coordinates may be inaccurate.
  • A report may be incomplete, exaggerated or deliberately misleading.
  • People without smartphones or reliable connectivity may remain underrepresented.

Authorities can improve reliability by checking timestamps and locations, comparing photographs with other observations, contacting reliable local sources and marking uncertain reports for further verification.

Indian example: Bhuvan mobile applications

NRSC describes the use of mobile applications for collecting location-based field information, geotagged photographs and other observations. Its disaster management work has included mobile applications for recording damaged assets and reporting incidents.

Such applications illustrate how local observations can be added to geospatial systems. Some field-data applications also support storing observations for later transmission where immediate connectivity is unavailable. However, the availability of a particular function depends on the application being used.

Satellite: Broad-area observation. Drone: Detailed observation of selected locations. Crowdsourcing: Reports contributed by people. Their combined value increases when observations are cross-checked.

Prelims focus

  • A camera-equipped drone can perform airborne remote sensing.
  • Geotagging links an observation to a geographic location.
  • Crowdsourcing collects information from multiple contributors.
  • Duplicate reports and incorrect locations are important crowdsourcing limitations.
  • NRSC's Bhuvan applications support location-based field-data collection.
  • Trap: A geotagged or widely shared photograph is not automatically an authenticated disaster report.

[Sources: NRSC, Bhuvan Mobile Applications, overview of location-based field-data collection and crowdsourcing; NRSC, Disaster Management Support, Applications and incident-reporting sections; consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.caption: Drones can support local damage assessment while keeping survey teams away from some hazardous areas.

title: Drones and Crowdsourcing: Collecting Information from Affected Areas

body:
What artificial intelligence can contribute

Artificial intelligence (AI) refers to computer systems designed to perform tasks that involve capabilities such as recognising patterns, interpreting information or generating predictions. In disaster management, AI can help analyse large quantities of information from satellites, monitoring instruments, historical records and field reports.

Machine learning is an important approach within AI. A machine-learning model identifies patterns from examples or other training data and uses those patterns when examining new information.

AI can assist disaster management, but it does not replace scientific monitoring, field verification or the responsibility of authorised institutions to make life-safety decisions.

Three major applications

Recognising patterns in images

AI-based image analysis may help identify features such as floodwater, damaged structures or changes in land cover. For example, a model can assist analysts by highlighting parts of a satellite image that may contain newly inundated land.

The highlighted area is a model output, not necessarily a verified fact. Cloud effects, shadows, unusual surfaces or differences between training data and actual conditions can create mistakes.

Supporting forecasts and risk assessments

AI can help analyse relationships in historical and current observations. It may support forecasting or the assessment of likely impacts where suitable data and validated models are available.

A prediction describes what may happen under the model's assumptions. It is different from an observation of what has already happened. Forecasts remain uncertain, and the degree of uncertainty may change as new information arrives.

Helping authorities compare priorities

AI and other analytical systems may help identify areas that appear to require urgent attention by combining hazard information with mapped exposure and available resources.

For example, a system might identify several settlements within an estimated flood zone. Officials must still check whether the information is current, whether residents need assistance and whether the proposed actions are feasible and safe.

Four distinct stages that should not be confused

StageMeaningExample
ObservationInformation about a measured or recorded conditionSatellite image showing water at an observed time
ForecastEstimate of a possible future conditionExpected movement or extent of a hazard
Risk assessmentEvaluation of possible harm to exposed and vulnerable people or assetsIdentification of settlements potentially affected
DecisionSelection of action by the responsible authorityIssuing an alert or arranging protective assistance

Understanding AI errors

A false positive occurs when a system identifies a condition that is not actually present. For example, an image classifier may mark a dry surface as flooded.

A false negative occurs when the system fails to identify a condition that is present. For example, it may fail to detect actual floodwater.

False positives can divert attention or resources. False negatives can leave people or locations without timely attention. Both errors matter, but their consequences differ according to the hazard and decision involved.

Why human oversight remains essential

AI performance depends on data quality, testing, the suitability of its training examples and the conditions in which it is used. A system trained mainly on one type of settlement or landscape may perform less reliably elsewhere.

For disaster-related decisions, responsible use requires suitable validation, clear accountability, monitoring for errors, attention to affected communities and human oversight. AI should strengthen the ability of scientific and administrative institutions to act, not conceal uncertainty or responsibility.

Prelims focus

  • Machine learning uses patterns in data to support analysis or prediction.
  • AI can assist with image interpretation, forecasting and risk assessment.
  • A model prediction is not an observed fact.
  • A false positive indicates a condition that is absent; a false negative misses a condition that is present.
  • Human oversight remains necessary for decisions affecting public safety.
  • Trap: An AI-generated assessment is not automatically an authorised disaster warning.

[Sources: UNDRR, World Meteorological Organization, International Telecommunication Union and International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, Leveraging AI to Enhance Multi-Hazard Early Warning Systems, 2026, report overview and recommendations on governance, observations and human oversight; NRSC, Disaster Management Support, Overview; consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Recorded evidence feeds AI analysis, followed by verification and responsible human review before public action; false positives and false negatives are contrasted.
pictures.caption: AI supports analysis, but decisions affecting human safety require accountable review.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Disaster Risk Assessment and Decision-Making

body:
From hazard detection to early warning

A forecast becomes useful for disaster risk reduction when people receive a trustworthy warning and have the knowledge and means to respond. This is why early warning is broader than weather forecasting or the transmission of a message.

An early warning system integrates hazard monitoring, forecasting, risk assessment, communication and preparedness so that people and institutions can take timely action before a hazardous event causes harm.

The four elements of a people-centred early warning system

  1. Disaster risk knowledge: Identify hazards, exposed populations, vulnerable locations and available capacities.
  2. Detection, monitoring, analysis and forecasting: Observe hazards and assess how conditions may develop.
  3. Warning dissemination and communication: Send authoritative, timely, understandable and actionable information to the people who need it.
  4. Preparedness to respond: Ensure that institutions and communities know what actions to take and can carry them out.

These elements must function together. A scientifically accurate cyclone forecast cannot by itself protect a household that receives no warning. A household that receives a warning also needs to understand the safe action required.

Role of telecommunications

Telecommunications enables information to move between authorities, emergency services and the public. Disaster communication may use mobile networks, radio, television, satellite communication, internet services, public announcement systems and local communication arrangements.

These channels serve different purposes. A mobile message may reach many people rapidly, while radio, public announcements and local volunteers may help communicate when internet access is limited.

Disasters can damage electricity supplies, communication towers, cables and other infrastructure. Preparedness therefore requires redundancy, meaning more than one suitable method of communicating essential information. A backup channel is valuable only if personnel know when and how to use it.

India's Common Alerting Protocol system

The Common Alerting Protocol (CAP) provides a standardised way to represent warning information so that an alert can be distributed through different communication systems. CAP is an information format and integration approach; it is not itself a weather-forecasting instrument or a siren.

The National Disaster Management Authority's SACHET National Disaster Alert Portal is part of India's CAP-based integrated alert system. It is designed to support geographically targeted, multilingual dissemination of warnings through multiple channels.

According to the portal's official description, warning information is generated by authorised agencies including the India Meteorological Department (IMD), Central Water Commission (CWC), Indian National Centre for Ocean Information Services (INCOIS) and other specified scientific and disaster management authorities.

The distinction between the warning originator and the dissemination platform is important: a platform can distribute an alert without being the agency that scientifically detected or forecast the hazard.

What makes a warning actionable?

An effective public warning should help recipients understand:

  • What hazard is expected or occurring.
  • Which area may be affected.
  • When the threat is relevant.
  • How serious the possible consequences may be.
  • What protective action is advised by the responsible authority.
  • Where to obtain further authoritative information.

Messages should be understandable to local communities, including people with disabilities, older persons and people with limited digital access. Communication needs may differ by language, location and available technology.

The importance of last-mile communication

Last-mile communication means ensuring that warnings reach the people who need them, including residents in remote or poorly connected areas. It involves more than sending a message from a central server.

Local authorities may need to confirm that warnings have been received and understood. Community volunteers, public announcements and established local networks can support this process. A missing mobile alert should never be treated as proof that no danger exists.

Source and date status: The official SACHET portal identified version 3.2.1 and reported its last update as 15 October 2026. The description here reflects the portal information available at the content cutoff of 2 November 2026; live alerts and implementation details can change.

Prelims focus

  • People-centred early warning systems have 4 interrelated elements.
  • Forecasting is only one part of an early warning system.
  • CAP standardises alert information for dissemination across different channels.
  • SACHET is an NDMA-associated national disaster alert platform.
  • IMD, CWC and INCOIS are among the agencies providing warning information through the integrated system.
  • Trap: Warning dissemination and scientific hazard forecasting are not the same institutional function.

[Sources: UNDRR, Disaster Risk Reduction Terminology, Early Warning System, four interrelated elements; NDMA, SACHET National Disaster Alert Portal, About and CAP Integrated Alert System sections, portal update stated as 15 October 2026; UNDRR, Inclusive Early Warning Early Action: Checklist and Implementation Guide, 2023, overview; consulted 2 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Four early warning elements form a connected cycle, improved by feedback; successful protection requires all four.
pictures.caption: Effective early warning requires all four connected elements, not forecasting alone.
